stem: A worm is spreading over SMB between workstations on a flat network. Which action stops the spread fastest?

options.text: Segment the network and block SMB between workstation subnets
options.why: Containment is a network decision. Cutting the path the worm uses stops propagation immediately, across every host at once.

options.text: Push the vendor patch to all workstations
options.why: Patching prevents the next outbreak. It takes time to deploy, requires reboots, and does nothing about hosts already infected.

options.text: Update antivirus definitions and run a scan on every host
options.why: Scanning is eradication, one host at a time, while the worm keeps reinfecting from neighbours.

options.text: Enable the host based firewall on each workstation individually
options.why: The right idea at the wrong layer and the wrong speed. Doing it per host during an active outbreak is far too slow.

stem: Which control automatically places a device that fails a posture check onto a restricted VLAN where it can only reach remediation servers?

options.text: Network access control
options.why: NAC evaluates device posture at connection time and can assign a quarantine VLAN automatically.

options.text: A next-generation firewall
options.why: It can enforce policy between segments once the device is placed, but it does not evaluate endpoint posture and assign VLANs.

options.text: Endpoint detection and response
options.why: EDR can isolate a host it considers compromised, but it is not the control that gates admission based on a posture check.

options.text: A SIEM correlation rule
options.why: A SIEM detects and alerts. It does not place devices on VLANs.

stem: A phishing email compromises one workstation, and the attacker then reaches the finance file server, the domain controller and a database within an hour. Which mitigation most directly addresses the part that went wrong after the initial compromise?

options.text: Network segmentation, to limit what a compromised host can reach
options.why: The failure described is lateral movement, not the initial entry. Segmentation bounds the blast radius, which is precisely the problem the hour of free movement reveals.

options.text: Patching the workstation
options.why: The entry was a phishing email, so a patch would not have prevented it, and it does nothing about the spread afterwards.

options.text: Monitoring to alert on unusual access
options.why: Monitoring would have told you it was happening. The question asks what addresses the movement itself, and detection is not prevention.

options.text: Encryption of the data on the file server
options.why: Transparent to an attacker using a valid session, and it does nothing to restrict reach.

stem: A marketing intern can open the HR disciplinary folder. Investigation shows the folder's access list grants the whole Staff group read access. What is the immediate fix, and what principle was violated?

options.text: Correct the permissions on the folder; the principle violated is least privilege
options.why: The immediate action is configuration: narrow the access list to the HR group. Least privilege is the principle that should have governed the grant in the first place.

options.text: Apply least privilege to the folder as a setting
options.why: Least privilege is a design principle, not a switch. It is the reason for the change rather than the change itself.

options.text: Encrypt the folder so only HR can read it
options.why: Workable in some designs and far heavier than needed. The access list already exists and is simply wrong.

options.text: Enable monitoring on the folder to detect further access
options.why: That tells you it keeps happening. It does not stop the intern opening the folder.

stem: Which of these mitigation techniques is detective rather than preventive?

options.text: Monitoring
options.why: Monitoring reports that something happened. Every other technique listed here acts to stop it, which is why a question asking how to prevent recurrence never answers with monitoring alone.

options.text: Segmentation
options.why: Preventive: it stops traffic reaching places it should not.

options.text: Patching
options.why: Preventive: it removes the flaw before it can be used.

options.text: Host-based intrusion prevention
options.why: The word prevention is in the name. An IDS would detect; an IPS blocks.

stem: Backup tapes are collected weekly by a courier. One is lost in transit. Which mitigation would have made the loss a logistics problem rather than a breach?

options.text: Encryption of the backup media
options.why: The exposure is disclosure of data outside your control. Encryption at rest on the media is the one control that still works once the tape is somewhere you are not.

options.text: Tighter permissions on the source file servers
options.why: Permissions govern access through the system. They travel nowhere with a physical tape.

options.text: Monitoring of backup job completion
options.why: Confirms the backup ran. It says nothing about what happens to the media afterwards.

options.text: Segmentation of the backup network
options.why: Reduces what can reach the backup infrastructure, and has no bearing on a tape in a van.

stem: A database server should only ever accept connections from two application servers, yet it currently accepts them from the entire user VLAN. Which mitigation applies most directly?

options.text: An access control list permitting only the two application servers to reach the database port
options.why: The failure is which traffic is permitted to reach a resource, which is exactly what an ACL governs. It is narrower and more precise than re-architecting segments.

options.text: Least privilege applied to the database accounts
options.why: That governs what an authenticated user may do once connected. The problem here is who can reach the port at all.

options.text: Endpoint protection on the database server
options.why: Aimed at malicious code executing on the host, not at which hosts may connect.

options.text: Encryption of the database connection
options.why: Protects the traffic from interception. Everyone who should not reach it still can.

stem: An application server runs software the vendor retired three years ago. It is still needed by one business process that is being replaced in eight months. Which combination is appropriate now?

options.text: Isolate it with strict access control and monitoring until it can be decommissioned on the planned date
options.why: No patch is coming, the system is still needed, and there is a known end date. Isolation plus a decommissioning plan is the expected pairing.

options.text: Patch it to the latest available version
options.why: There are no further versions. The vendor retired it.

options.text: Decommission it immediately
options.why: A business process still depends on it. Mitigation has to carry it to the replacement date rather than break the business today.

options.text: Install endpoint protection and consider the risk addressed
options.why: Helpful and insufficient on its own. It does not reduce who can reach an unpatchable service.

stem: A finance workstation executes a malicious macro that drops and runs an unsigned binary. Which mitigation is designed to stop that chain on the host itself?

options.text: Endpoint protection installed on the workstation
options.why: Detecting and blocking malicious execution on the host is exactly its remit, including the behavioural chain of a document spawning a process.

options.text: A host-based firewall
options.why: Controls which network connections the host accepts and makes. It does not inspect what executes locally.

options.text: Network segmentation
options.why: Limits where the host can go afterwards. The binary still runs.

options.text: Encryption of the finance share
options.why: Transparent to a process running as the logged-on user.

stem: A service account used by a reporting tool holds domain administrator rights because that was simplest at install. Which TWO responses address this correctly? (Choose two.)

options.text: Reduce the account's permissions to exactly what the reporting tool requires
options.why: The immediate configuration fix. Everything else is secondary while the account can do anything in the domain.

options.text: Adopt least privilege as the standard for service account provisioning, so this is not repeated
options.why: The principle that prevents the next one. Fixing one account without changing how accounts are granted guarantees a repeat.

options.text: Patch the reporting tool to its latest version
options.why: Good practice and unrelated. The flaw is the rights granted, not the software version.

options.text: Encrypt the reporting tool's configuration file
options.why: Protects a stored credential, and leaves the account's excessive rights exactly as they were.

options.text: Enable monitoring of the service account's activity and consider it resolved
options.why: Monitoring is worth having alongside the fix. On its own it watches a problem rather than removing it.

stem: A medical device runs an operating system the manufacturer will not patch and cannot be replaced this year. Which TWO are appropriate compensating controls? (Choose two.)

options.text: Place the device on an isolated VLAN reachable only by the one server it must talk to
options.why: The control you wanted is unavailable, so network isolation meets the objective another way. That is what makes it compensating.

options.text: Monitor the segment and alert on any traffic outside the one permitted flow
options.why: Detection substitutes for the prevention you cannot deploy, and it is recorded against the documented exception.

options.text: Apply the latest vendor patch
options.why: The scenario states there is none. This is the control that is unavailable, which is why a compensating one is needed.

options.text: Accept the risk and record it in the register with no further action
options.why: That is acceptance, not compensation. Acceptance leaves the exposure exactly as it was.

options.text: Install endpoint protection agents on the device
options.why: An unpatchable legacy OS generally cannot run a current agent, which is part of why it needs isolating.

stem: A requirement states that no unapproved software may execute, including software the company has never seen before. Which control meets it?

options.text: An application allow list
options.why: Only permitted software runs, so anything unknown is blocked by default. This is the same logic as a firewall's implicit deny.

options.text: An application deny list of known-bad software
options.why: A deny list permits anything it has no entry for, so it cannot make a promise about software nobody has seen.

options.text: Signature based antivirus with current definitions
options.why: Also an enumerate-the-bad approach. No definition exists for the unseen.

options.text: A host based firewall
options.why: That governs network connections, not which binaries may execute.

stem: A server is fully patched. Which hardening steps still reduce its attack surface?

options.text: Removing unnecessary software, disabling unused services and changing default credentials
options.why: Patching fixes known flaws in what you run. Hardening reduces what you run and what it exposes, including tomorrow's flaw in software you did not need.

options.text: None; a fully patched host is hardened by definition
options.why: A fully patched host with default credentials and every service enabled is still trivially compromised. No patch fixes a default password.

options.text: Only installing additional monitoring
options.why: Monitoring detects. It removes no attack surface.

options.text: Increasing the patch cadence further
options.why: More of the thing already done, and it still does not touch unnecessary services or default credentials.

stem: Which hardening measure blocks malicious behaviour on the host itself rather than filtering its network connections?

options.text: A host based intrusion prevention system
options.why: HIPS watches activity on the host and blocks behaviour it judges malicious, which is a different layer from connection filtering.

options.text: A host based firewall
options.why: That is exactly the network connection filtering the question excludes.

options.text: Disabling unused ports
options.why: Also a network exposure measure, and a static one.

options.text: Network segmentation
options.why: Segmentation happens between hosts, not on one.

stem: An internet-facing server runs an application the vendor stopped supporting two years ago and the business no longer uses. What is the appropriate mitigation?

options.text: Decommission it
options.why: Unused and unsupportable. Removing it eliminates the exposure entirely, which no control applied to a live host can match.

options.text: Isolate it on its own segment and monitor it
options.why: The right answer when the business still needs the system. It does not, so compensating controls are unnecessary cost and residual risk.

options.text: Apply the latest available patches
options.why: There are none; support ended two years ago.

options.text: Add a web application firewall in front of it
options.why: A compensating control for something you must keep running. You do not have to keep this running.

stem: Which statement correctly contrasts an application allow list with a deny list?

options.text: An allow list enumerates what may run and blocks everything else; a deny list enumerates what may not and permits everything else
options.why: The default is what separates them, and it is why only the allow list can make a promise about software nobody has catalogued.

options.text: They are equivalent, differing only in how the list is written
options.why: They have opposite defaults. One fails closed on the unknown, the other fails open.

options.text: A deny list is stronger because it names the actual threats
options.why: Naming threats means the list is only ever as current as the last update, and the set of bad software is unbounded.

options.text: An allow list requires less up-front effort than a deny list
options.why: Reversed. An allow list costs more up front, because every legitimate program must be catalogued. On a fixed-function system it then stays stable, while a deny list needs endless updating and is always behind.

stem: A hospital lobby kiosk runs a single browser in full screen. Nothing else must ever execute on it, including malware that has not been written yet, and the team wants the least ongoing maintenance. Which approach fits?

options.text: A deny list of known malicious executables, updated daily
options.why: A deny list only blocks what is already named. Malware written tomorrow is not on today's list, and the daily updates are endless maintenance.

options.text: Antivirus with heuristic scanning enabled
options.why: Heuristics raise the odds of catching new malware, but anything that slips past them still runs. Only default deny makes the promise in the stem.

options.text: A deny list of administrative tools such as command shells and scripting hosts
options.why: Removing a few dangerous tools shrinks the attack surface, but every program not on that short list still runs freely.

options.text: An application allow list containing only the browser and the operating system components it needs
options.why: Everything not on the list is blocked by default, including software nobody has seen, and a single-purpose device has a short, stable list.

stem: An auditor finds that every developer on a payroll system still holds production database administrator rights, granted when the system was built three years ago and never reviewed. Which principle should govern the remediation?

options.text: Permissions: set each developer's permissions to read only
options.why: Permissions are the configuration you will change, not the principle that decides the target. Read only may itself be more than some developers need in production.

options.text: Access control lists: attach an ACL to the database
options.why: An ACL is the structure the rights are recorded in. The database already has one; what it holds is the problem, and a principle decides what it should hold.

options.text: Encryption of the database, so developers cannot read the data
options.why: Administrators of the database can typically manage its keys and its data. The problem is the access granted, not whether the data is encrypted.

options.text: Least privilege: each role receives only the access it needs, so the standing production rights are removed
options.why: The question asks for the principle that decides how much to grant. The fix will change permissions, but least privilege is what tells you what they should be.

stem: Switch administration on an access layer uses Telnet. A packet capture taken from a compromised laptop on the management VLAN shows administrator usernames and passwords in readable form. Which mitigation removes this exposure?

options.text: Require longer administrator passwords on every switch
options.why: Length does not matter when the password crosses the wire in readable form. The capture shows the failure is the protocol, not the password.

options.text: Alert on every Telnet login to the switches
options.why: An alert reports the exposure after it has happened. Monitoring never prevents the credentials being read.

options.text: Disable Telnet and manage the switches over SSH
options.why: Turning off the cleartext protocol removes the opening, and SSH encrypts the session so a capture shows nothing useful.

options.text: Apply the latest firmware to every switch model
options.why: Firmware fixes flaws in what runs. It does not reduce what runs, so Telnet would stay enabled and still expose passwords.

stem: Sales staff work from cafes and hotels on company laptops, so the corporate firewall never sees their traffic. Another guest at a hotel found file sharing reachable on one laptop. Which mitigation protects the laptop wherever it is?

options.text: Enable the host firewall and block inbound file sharing
options.why: A firewall on the laptop travels with it and filters connections wherever the laptop connects, which is the traffic path that failed.

options.text: Add a rule to the headquarters firewall blocking file sharing
options.why: The laptop's traffic never passes the headquarters firewall, so a rule there blocks nothing. A blocking device out of the path cannot stop the traffic.

options.text: Install a network intrusion detection sensor at headquarters
options.why: A sensor at headquarters sees neither the hotel network nor the laptop, and a detection device only watches, it does not stop traffic.

options.text: Encrypt every laptop's disk with a strong key and a PIN
options.why: Disk encryption protects a powered-off or stolen device. The failure here was a service reachable over the network.

stem: A vendor releases a security patch for the runtime that the company's application servers need. Last quarter an emergency patch applied to every production server at once broke the order system. How should the team deploy this patch?

options.text: Apply it to every server tonight to close the gap quickly
options.why: Applying untested to everything at once is how the last outage happened. Without a test or a way back, an unexpected side effect reaches every server.

options.text: Skip it and add monitoring to the unpatched servers
options.why: Monitoring shows an attack and prevents nothing. The flaw would stay in the runtime the servers depend on.

options.text: Remove unneeded services from the servers instead of patching
options.why: Hardening reduces what runs, but the runtime is required, so the flawed code stays. Patching fixes what you run.

options.text: Test it first, then roll out in stages with rollback ready
options.why: Testing finds the side effect before production, and staging limits its reach. A rollback means a failure can be undone.

stem: A scan finds that 40 of 400 servers have no endpoint protection agent, although policy requires one on every server. Most of the 40 were built in the last two months. Which action stops the gap from recurring?

options.text: Email server owners a reminder to install the agent
options.why: A reminder is a document, not a control. Nothing detects or corrects a server that is built without the agent.

options.text: Add the agent to the standard build and report any drift
options.why: Building the agent into the image means new servers start protected, and drift reporting shows any that lose it. It is a continuous control.

options.text: Run the same scan monthly instead of quarterly
options.why: Scanning more often finds the gap sooner but does not close it. A scan is a detective control and the servers would still be built without the agent.

options.text: Raise the alert sensitivity on the agents already installed
options.why: More sensitive alerts on protected servers do nothing for the servers that have no agent at all.

stem: An attacker found a building's network cameras online and logged in with the manufacturer's published login. The cameras ran current firmware. Which mitigation addresses the cause?

options.text: Change every default credential during installation
options.why: The login that worked was the factory default, so replacing it during deployment removes the opening the attacker used.

options.text: Update the camera firmware on a quarterly schedule
options.why: The cameras were already current. A fully patched device with default credentials is still trivially taken over.

options.text: Review the camera login logs for odd activity weekly
options.why: Reviewing logs finds a takeover after it happened and prevents nothing. The failed control is the credential.

options.text: Block the network addresses the attacker came from
options.why: A list of known bad addresses is endless and the attacker can use another. The weakness is still there for the next one.

stem: A retired reporting server was switched off and left in a rack. Six months later an attacker signed in to the network with the server's old service account, and a firewall rule still permitted traffic to its address. What was missed?

options.text: The server should have been patched before it was shut down
options.why: A patch on a powered-off server changes nothing. The attack used leftover access, not a flaw in the server's software.

options.text: The server should have been moved to an isolated VLAN
options.why: Isolating a server that is already off does not remove the account or the rule. Neither of them depended on the server being on.

options.text: The decommissioning left the account and the rule in place
options.why: Retiring a system includes removing its accounts, rules and records so that nothing still grants access to it.

options.text: Monitoring should have been enabled on the powered-off server
options.why: A powered-off server produces no events to monitor. The access lived in the account and the firewall rule.

stem: A contractor needs to read one quarterly report for the next two weeks. The finance share also holds payroll and tax files. Which access grant follows least privilege?

options.text: Add the contractor to the finance group for the month
options.why: Group membership gives everything the group can reach, including payroll and tax files the contractor does not need.

options.text: Copy the finance manager's access to the contractor's account
options.why: The manager's access is far wider than one report, so copying it grants far more than the task needs.

options.text: Give read and write on the whole share, then remove it later
options.why: Granting broad access now and relying on a later cleanup is the opposite of granting only what is needed.

options.text: Grant read on that one report, with an expiry in two weeks
options.why: The grant covers exactly the file and the action needed, and it ends when the need does.

stem: Over three weeks an attacker guessed passwords against the VPN from addresses in many countries, mostly at night, until one worked. Nothing alerted anyone and an outside party found the breach. Which mitigation would have shortened detection?

options.text: Require a longer minimum length for all VPN user passwords
options.why: A longer password may make guessing slower, but it is a preventive control and does not make anyone notice the attempts.

options.text: Alert on abnormal sign-ins in the authentication logs
options.why: A flood of failures from many countries is visible in the logs. An alert on it turns that record into early warning.

options.text: Turn on data loss prevention across the file servers
options.why: That watches data leaving, not people signing in. It would not see the guessing against the VPN.

options.text: Encrypt the VPN connection with a stronger cipher suite
options.why: The attacker signed in with a valid password, so the strength of the cipher did not matter and no one was alerted.

stem: A power utility's control network must send readings to the corporate network in one direction, continuously, so that planners can see them. Management proposes an air gap for the control network. Which design best mitigates the risk?

options.text: Put both networks in one VLAN and restrict the corporate hosts
options.why: Sharing a network gives corporate hosts a path to the controllers. The failure to avoid is too much reachability, and this keeps it.

options.text: Air gap the control network, with a permanent cable for readings
options.why: A permanent cable is a connection, so it is not an air gap. If data has to keep moving, the design is logical segmentation.

options.text: Segment the network behind a firewall permitting one flow
options.why: Segmentation with one permitted flow meets the requirement that data keep moving, and everything else is denied.

options.text: Install endpoint protection on every controller
options.why: Controllers that run a physical process usually cannot take an agent. The fitting control is isolation, not something installed on the device.

stem: A project folder's access list names 40 individual users. People who moved to other teams still have access, and someone must edit the list by hand for every joiner and leaver. Which change fixes the cause?

options.text: Review the list every year and remove the old names
options.why: A yearly review catches leavers late, and the manual editing that created the problem stays. It treats the symptom.

options.text: Make the folder read-only for every single user
options.why: Least privilege means the access each role needs, not none. A read-only rule also stops people who must edit.

options.text: Move the folder to an encrypted storage volume
options.why: Encrypting the volume protects a stolen disk. The people who should not have access are authorized users of the share.

options.text: Grant access to groups that follow HR role changes
options.why: Permissions tied to groups follow role changes automatically, so leavers lose access when their role changes.

stem: A retailer's card payment servers share a flat network with office laptops, so an audit would have to cover every device. The company wants to shrink what must meet the strictest controls and limit what a compromised laptop can reach. Which mitigation fits?

options.text: Place the payment servers in their own tight segment
options.why: A separate segment limits what a laptop can reach and keeps the strict controls to the devices inside it.

options.text: Encrypt all internal traffic between office laptops
options.why: Encryption protects data on the wire between laptops. It does not change which devices can reach the payment servers.

options.text: Install endpoint protection on the office laptops only
options.why: An agent may stop some malware but does not limit reach, and every device would still be in scope.

options.text: Deploy a list of known bad addresses at the network edge
options.why: An edge list of bad addresses does nothing about traffic between internal devices on a flat network.

stem: Monitoring confirms that a file server is sending data to an unknown external address. The team wants to stop the transfer and keep evidence. Which TWO actions should it take first? (Choose two.)

options.text: Move the server to a quarantine VLAN with no egress
options.why: Isolation cuts the path while the server stays running, so memory and logs are kept for analysis.

options.text: Power the server off to stop the transfer at once
options.why: Powering off ends the transfer but loses volatile evidence such as memory. Disconnect, do not power off.

options.text: Reimage the server before collecting anything from it
options.why: Rebuilding comes after containment and after evidence is collected. Done first, it destroys what the investigation needs.

options.text: Block the server's outbound traffic at the firewall
options.why: A rule at the egress point stops the data leaving without touching the server, so the evidence stays intact.

options.text: Run a full antivirus scan and leave it online
options.why: Scanning is cleaning, one host at a time, while the transfer continues. Containment comes first.

stem: A fleet of 60 network printers ships with the default administrator password, and with unused FTP, SMB and wireless direct services enabled. Which TWO mitigations remove these weaknesses? (Choose two.)

options.text: Apply the latest firmware update to every printer
options.why: Firmware fixes flaws in the code, but it leaves the default password and the unused services in place. Patching fixes what you run, hardening reduces it.

options.text: Replace the default admin password on each printer
options.why: The factory password is published, so replacing it closes the easiest way in.

options.text: Install an endpoint protection agent on each printer
options.why: Printers are appliances that normally cannot run an agent. A device that cannot be changed that way needs another control.

options.text: Review printer logs for administrator logins monthly
options.why: Reading logs after the fact prevents nothing, and the weaknesses would remain.

options.text: Disable the unused FTP, SMB and wireless services
options.why: A service that is off cannot be attacked. This reduces the attack surface.

stem: After a web server was breached, investigators found that the attacker compiled a tool on it using a compiler left from the build process, then used a debugger to read process memory. Neither is needed in production. Which mitigation would have denied the attacker these tools?

options.text: Patch the compiler and debugger to current versions
options.why: A patched compiler still compiles. The problem is that the tools are present, not that they have flaws.

options.text: Remove the compiler and debugger from the image
options.why: Software that is not installed cannot be misused, and production has no need for build tools.

options.text: Add the tool names to a deny list on the server
options.why: A list of banned names is easy to get around, for instance by renaming a binary. Removing the tools is what denies them.

options.text: Alert when the compiler or debugger is started
options.why: An alert shows the misuse after it starts and stops nothing. The tools would remain available.
